blocks.text: THINK  What are the disadvantages if we do not spend time and effort in identifying and documenting requirements? Pause and write down your responses before reading further.

If we do not spend sufficient time and effort identifying and documenting requirements, there is a mismatch between what the user expects and what the developer builds. Time, effort and money are spent on something the customer did not ask for, changes are needed, there are more iterations, and development cost rises significantly.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Why do requirements matter?

rows: Simple meaning  Requirement gathering asks: “What does the customer need?” Requirement analysis checks: “Do we understand that need correctly?”

blocks.text: Importance of requirement gathering and analysis is two-fold: (1) developers understand what customers want — how the software should look and behave; (2) customers come to an agreement that the developers' understanding matches what they expect. Otherwise cost, time and iterations increase.

Remember, the customer is not always the end user — it can be an internal user or someone from a different team. First teams gather requirements, then analyse them, and only after that think about how to develop the software.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Why do requirements matter?

sections.title: Who should we ask? Stakeholders and users

blocks.text: When a software system is introduced it influences different types of users — from your own organisation, other organisations or end users, with different roles and profiles. All these users are called stakeholders. We must understand their requirements in a broad, holistic manner before designing.
EXAMPLE  Amazon wants to develop a portal for sellers. Products which sellers list on the portal will be available for people to buy on Amazon.

blocks.text: During requirements analysis, we analyse the gathered requirements to form a clear understanding of the exact customer requirements and to weed out any problems. Problems arise because requirements come from various stakeholders and different sources.
THINK  What kind of problems or issues can arise from the gathered requirements? Pause and write down your responses before reading further.
Ambiguous requirements

“Independent sellers need to manage their inventory”: manage could mean add a product, modify a price, delete products… Developers build based on their own interpretation, so we must ensure the idea of what is required is the same from the user’s and the developer’s perspective.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Requirement analysis: spotting problems

blocks.text: Inconsistent requirements

Independent sellers want payment credited every week; the banking system allows only credit every two weeks. Developers must resolve this, e.g. tell sellers this is what can be provided; once people know the constraints, you can build.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Requirement analysis: spotting problems

blocks.text: Incomplete requirements

Some aspects were overlooked because neither customer nor developer could imagine all details. “Track orders”: delivered orders, orders in transit, or returned orders? The developer needs this before proceeding.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Requirement analysis: spotting problems

blocks.text: REMEMBER  Analysis of requirements is essential to identify ambiguities, inconsistencies and incomplete requirements. Then we are in a better position to start designing the system.

Users identified for the Seller Portal: independent sellers, sales team/manager of companies, advertising department, logistics/shipping company manager, buyers, banks. How do we gather requirements from them?

THINK  You have been commissioned by Amazon to build the Seller Portal. How do we gather requirements from independent sellers, sales teams/managers, the advertising department, logistics/shipping managers, buyers and banks? Pause and write down your responses before reading further.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Five ways to gather requirements

blocks.text: Questionnaires

A series of questions designed to elicit specific information from users. Answers can be yes/no, a choice from a set of answers, or a longer response/comment. Good for getting answers to specific questions from a large group of people, usually spread across a wide geographical area.

EXAMPLE  Send to sales team managers of several mobile companies: “What percentage of your inventory do you sell online?” “What are the main difficulties you encounter in selling your product online?”
Questionnaires should be used in conjunction with other techniques.

blocks.caption: A questionnaire sent to sales managers of several mobile companies.
blocks.alt: A questionnaire sent to sales managers of several mobile companies.

blocks.text: Interviews

Asking someone a set of questions — face-to-face, telephonic or online. Classified as structured, unstructured or semi-structured depending on how rigorously the interviewer sticks to a prepared set of questions. Structured: a fixed set of questions. Unstructured: the interviewer does not know what questions to ask because they don't know what the user does or needs, so they ask broad questions and probe further based on responses.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Questionnaires and interviews

blocks.text: Getting people to explore issues; used early in requirement gathering to elicit scenarios.

EXAMPLE  Ask independent sellers “What other platforms do you use to sell your products? Advantages/disadvantages?” They may say WhatsApp, Instagram — easy to get customers, but tracking orders, payments, inventory and selling options is a huge overhead. Requirement: tracking orders, payments, inventory, selling options.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Questionnaires and interviews

sections.title: Focus groups, observation and existing documents

blocks.text: Focus groups

Drawback of interviews: they offer only one perspective. Alternative: get a group of stakeholders to discuss issues and requirements. Advantages: gaining consensus (if different groups highlight the same issue, it is a key requirement) and highlighting areas of conflict or disagreement.

EXAMPLE  Sales team managers from different verticals — the mobile sales team wants the sales summary on launch day; furniture wants the sales summary of the last 30 days. Requirement: sales summary for a specific day or the last x days.

blocks.caption: Different verticals, different needs → sales summary for a specific day or the last x days.
blocks.alt: Different verticals, different needs → sales summary for a specific day or the last x days.

blocks.text: Naturalistic observation

What people say is often different from what they do, and it is difficult to describe accurately how we do a task (e.g. how do buyers buy online?). So we spend time with stakeholders as they go about their day-to-day tasks, observing their work in its natural setting — shadowing a stakeholder, making notes, occasionally asking questions, but primarily observing.
EXAMPLE  How people sell in physical shops — shopkeeper/customer recommendations and customer feedback. Requirements: recommendations for what other items to sell; getting timely customer feedback.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Focus groups, observation and existing documents

blocks.text: Documentation

Procedures and rules for a task, steps involved in an activity, regulations governing a task. Example — bank regulations: How can you add sellers' bank accounts to your portal? How frequently can you deposit money to seller accounts? Also, practices of other online marketplaces.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Focus groups, observation and existing documents

blocks.alt: Illustration: Functional versus non-functional requirements

blocks.text: Functional requirements

Captures a functionality required by the users from the system: the user performs actions/gives inputs and the system provides an appropriate output. Like a mathematical function f: I → O transforming an element of the input domain I to a value in the output O. Functional requirements should clearly describe each functionality the system supports, with its corresponding input and output data set.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Functional versus non-functional requirements

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements
Non-functional requirements essentially specify how the system should behave, not what the system should do. Requirement 2 cannot be expressed as accepting input and producing output.

sections.title: Reliability, robustness and other quality requirements

blocks.text: THINK  What are some non-functional requirements for the Amazon Seller Portal? Pause and write down your responses before reading further.

Reliability is the extent to which a program behaves the same way over time in the same operating environment. E.g. the software should not crash often, otherwise users get frustrated; in the Seller Portal we must ensure the portal handles all operations, especially when the inventory changes based on buying and selling.

Robustness is the extent to which a program can recover from errors or unexpected input. E.g. a user gives garbage as input; in the Seller Portal the service must handle large numbers and high traffic.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Reliability, robustness and other quality requirements

blocks.text: When we specify reliability and robustness, we are ensuring the system behaves the way we intend — not specifying what the system should do. That is the key difference between functional and non-functional requirements.
Others: performance, portability, security, interoperability, etc.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Reliability, robustness and other quality requirements

blocks.text: In the Plan and Document perspective, requirement gathering and analysis is usually done by a system analyst, with other members of the software team. The analyst then organises the requirements in a Software Requirements Specification (SRS) document, which contains all the user requirements in a structured form.

2.1 Product perspective; 2.2 Product functions; 2.3 User characteristics; 2.4 Constraints; 2.5 Assumptions and dependencies
For each: introduction/purpose of feature; Stimulus/response sequence; associated functional requirements

blocks.text: Sections 1 and 2 give a broad outline and description of the system. Section 3 contains specific functional and non-functional requirements; 3.3–3.6 cover non-functional requirements like performance and security.
This is a guideline; based on the organisation and context, modifications to the structure and content are possible.

blocks.text: THINK  What are the advantages of maintaining an SRS document? Pause and write down your responses before reading further.
Advantages of an SRS

rows: Forms an agreement between customers and developers
The SRS is given to customers, who read it, and after several iterations it is accepted; customers know what to expect and developers know what customers expect.
Forces stakeholders to rigorously think about all requirements before design and development, reducing changes later.
Provides a basis for estimating costs and schedules
The size of the software is a function of all requirements; effort and cost are estimated from size, and the project manager creates a schedule from these estimates.
A basis for planning future enhancements.

blocks.text: Drawback: A lot of documentation is required. This is fine if the requirements are fixed.

blocks.caption: SRS advantages and its drawback.
blocks.alt: SRS advantages and drawback: a lot of documentation is required; this is fine if requirements are fixed.

sections.title: Plan and Document versus Agile requirements

blocks.text: The SRS serves as an agreement between customers and developers. But in many projects customers are unsure of the requirements, and their understanding evolves over time. The Agile perspective addresses this: working closely and interacting frequently with stakeholders to develop and refine requirements, building a working prototype and refining it by adding features in sprints/iterations (typically every 2 weeks). In Agile we are basically in maintenance mode as soon as we have some requirements. The Agile lifecycle begins with Behaviour Driven Design.

Behaviour Driven Design (BDD) asks questions about the behaviour of an application before and during development, so that stakeholders are less likely to miscommunicate. Requirements are still written down, but they are continuously refined to meet stakeholders' requirements and expectations. The BDD version of requirements is user stories, which take the place of the SRS in the Plan and Document perspective.

blocks.caption: BDD: ask about behaviour, write user stories, build in sprints, refine continuously.
blocks.alt: BDD: ask about behaviour, write user stories, build in sprints, refine continuously.

blocks.text: User stories are short, informal, plain-language descriptions of what a user wants to do within a software product, which is of value to them. They come from the Human Computer Interaction (HCI) community and are written on 3-inch by 5-inch (3×5) index cards. A user story is the smallest unit of work that can be done in 1 sprint (roughly 1–2 weeks).
The role-feature-benefit pattern
As a [type of user], I want [an action], so that [a benefit/value].

blocks.alt: Illustration: The user-story template

blocks.text: EXAMPLE  Feature: View inventory — As an independent seller, I want to view my inventory so that I can take stock of products which are low in number.
EXAMPLE  Feature: Track customer feedback — As an independent seller, I want to view my customers' feedback for each product so that I can get a sense of pertinent issues in my products.

blocks.alt: Illustration: The user-story template

blocks.text: Benefits of user stories

rows: E.g. the client may want catalogue and inventory first, so the team tells customers “we will provide the View inventory feature in 2 weeks.”
We do not tell customers how we will implement features, which reduces misunderstanding between stakeholders.
Conversation between users and the development team
This back-and-forth brings better, simpler, more valuable solutions.

blocks.alt: Illustration: Why are user stories useful?

blocks.text: EXAMPLE  When the Track customer feedback feature is shown, the client realises: 'I would also like to be notified by email about 1 or 2 star ratings of my product.' Such modifications are common in the Agile perspective, and user stories facilitate them.

blocks.caption: Conversation refines the story: email alerts for 1–2 star ratings.
blocks.alt: Conversation refines the story: email alerts for 1–2 star ratings.

blocks.text: A good user story should be SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Timeboxed.

rows: Each story is testable: known expected results for some inputs
Ideally implementable in one agile iteration (1–2 weeks), otherwise subdivide
Business value to one or more stakeholders
Stop implementing a feature once the time budget is exceeded

blocks.caption: SMART user stories.
blocks.alt: SMART user stories.

sections.title: SMART: how to improve a story

blocks.text: Specific
Vague: “User can search for a product in the catalogue” → specific: “User can search for a product by title in the catalogue”.
Measurable
Not measurable: “The Seller portal should have good response time” → measurable: “When adding a product to the catalogue, the product should appear in the catalogue within 3 seconds”.

blocks.alt: Illustration: SMART: how to improve a story

blocks.text: Achievable
“Feature 1: View inventory” → “Feature 1a: View all products in inventory in a single page” + “Feature 1b: Add pagination and filters”.
Relevant
Ask “Why is this feature needed?” and “So what?”
Timeboxed
If the time budget is exceeded: give up, divide the story into smaller ones, or reschedule what is left according to a new estimate.

blocks.alt: Illustration: SMART: how to improve a story

sections.title: User-story limits and choosing an approach

blocks.text: THINK  What are drawbacks of user stories? Pause and write down your responses before reading further.
1. Continuous contact with customers may be difficult or too expensive — customers may not want to participate or may not be available at all times.

2. May not scale to very large projects or safety-critical applications — these need extensive planning and documentation before implementation, and safety-critical applications have no room for errors or refinement.
REMEMBER  Software development methodologies depend on the type of application you are building.

blocks.text: A seller wants to “track orders.” What clarifying question would you ask?
A sales manager receives reports through the sales team. Primary, secondary or tertiary user?
Is “the product should appear within 5 seconds” functional or non-functional?
Why might a focus group reveal something that separate interviews do not?
Write one user story for a seller wanting an email alert about low product ratings.
How could you divide “View inventory” into smaller stories?
Suggested answers and reasoning
Answer 1: Which orders to track: delivered, in transit, or returned?
Answer 2: Secondary in the chapter classification: the manager receives the output indirectly through the sales team.
Answer 3: Non-functional — it specifies how the system should behave.
Answer 4: A focus group brings several stakeholders together, so it helps gain consensus and highlights areas of conflict or disagreement; an interview offers only one perspective.
Answer 5: As an independent seller, I want an email when a product receives a 1- or 2-star rating, so that I can investigate possible problems quickly.
Answer 6: Feature 1a: View all products in inventory in a single page; Feature 1b: Add pagination and filters.
